mcqs.question: Why does an API gateway's availability requirement need to match or exceed the platform as a whole, rather than just matching a typical backend service?
options: Gateway availability requirements are unrelated to backend requirements
Backends are always less reliable than gateways by default
Because every request passes through the gateway, its uptime becomes the platform's effective availability ceiling — even flawless backends can't exceed it
The gateway only needs high availability during business hours
mcqs.explanation: Since all traffic funnels through the gateway, its availability caps what the whole platform can achieve, regardless of how reliable individual backends are — a gateway with 99.9% uptime limits the entire platform to at most 99.9%, even if every backend is more reliable than that. There's no time-of-day exemption, and the two are very much related, not independent.

mcqs.question: Why do many platforms run both a central API gateway and a service-mesh sidecar pattern, rather than choosing one exclusively?
options: The two serve different traffic shapes — a gateway fits north-south (client-to-backend) traffic, a mesh fits east-west (service-to-service) traffic
Running both is only done for redundancy in case one fails
Service meshes are strictly a replacement for gateways and shouldn't be combined
A gateway can only handle authentication, while a mesh handles all routing
mcqs.explanation: The two solve different problems: a gateway sits at the platform's external edge, a mesh handles internal service-to-service traffic — they aren't redundant copies of the same function, they cover different traffic shapes. A gateway isn't limited to authentication, and a mesh doesn't strictly replace a gateway's edge role.

mcqs.question: Why does gateway latency have an outsized effect on the platform compared to a single backend service's latency?
options: Gateway latency is added on top of every single request in the system, so any inefficiency there is paid by every request regardless of which backend it targets
Gateway latency only affects requests that fail authentication
Backend latency is always more significant than gateway latency by definition
Gateway latency and backend latency are measured completely separately and never combine
mcqs.explanation: Because the gateway sits on every request's path, its added latency compounds across the entire platform's traffic, unlike a single backend's latency which only affects requests to that one service. It's not limited to failed-auth requests, backend latency isn't inherently larger by definition, and the two latencies do combine — gateway overhead adds on top of whatever the backend takes.
